headline: A drone and a dog are checking on 76 orcas.
summary: Seventy-six Southern Resident orcas are left in the waters off Washington and British Columbia. Scientists from the SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance fly a drone through a whale's spout to catch breath droplets, and a dog named Eba sniffs out droppings from the bow. A lab turns each sample into a health record.

cover_question.q: Why are there only 76 orcas left?

cover_answer: Their salmon got scarce. Dams, nets, noise, toxins.
table_question: Is it your job to fix a mess made before you were born?

5-7.script: Scientists near Seattle are checking on 76 orcas, the big black-and-white whales, to see if they're healthy. When an orca breathes out, the spray is as wide as a basketball, and a little flying robot catches a bit of it. A dog named Eba sniffs the air from the boat to find whale poop. The whales don't mind; to them the drone is just a funny seagull.
5-7.why: A dog that sniffs for whale poop is the whole story at this age, and it's true. The basketball makes the spout real. Give them the dog and the seagull, and leave the dams for later.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old takes one vivid thing for the whole event, so the script hands them the dog and the basketball-wide spout and leaves the dams and dead calves out. The whales shrugging at the drone like a seagull is the reassurance, in a picture. Expect 'can I see one?' Not from here, but the scientists can, and that's their job.

8-12.script: The Southern Resident orcas eat Chinook salmon. A century of dams and overfishing shrank those salmon from over 100 pounds to about 12. Hungry whales lose calves. So scientists catch each whale's spout with a drone and its droppings with a dog, and build it a health file like your doctor's.
8-12.why: Dams to small salmon to hungry whales: a chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child is working out cause and effect and wants to know whether the grown-ups are fixing it. The chain is dams, small salmon, hungry whales, lost calves; the health file is the fix they can picture, because they have seen their own. Expect 'is it working?' Honest answer: the checkups work, the fish are still missing.

13-17.script: Why do the orcas that eat seals thrive while the salmon-eaters die out in the same water? Bigg's orcas calve every two years; the Southern Residents miscarry, and their salmon have shrunk from over 100 pounds to about 12. Second: Deborah Giles says the job is to "turn back the clock." Who pays?
13-17.why: Seal-eaters against salmon-eaters: a comparison they can run alone.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the drone checkups are good work, and 76 whales with miscarrying mothers means the work is losing. The Bigg's orcas in the same water make the comparison theirs to run. Expect 'so what's the point of the checkups?' Giles's answer: when one whale needs help, they have its whole record.

5-7.q: Why do they want whale poop?
5-7.a: It shows if the whale is healthy, like a doctor's test.

8-12.q: Can't they just give the whales more fish?
8-12.a: Not by hand. The fix is bringing the salmon back.

8-12.q: How can a dog smell whale poop?
8-12.a: She sniffs the wind from the bow and whines when she has it.

13-17.q: Why are there only 76 orcas left?
13-17.a: Their salmon got small and scarce. Hungry females miscarry.
They glance at it and keep swimming, the pilot says.
